The White trevally, Pseudocaranx dentex, is a coastal carangid that achieves a maximum recorded total length of 122 centimetres [Li = 122 centimetres]. Studies of adult specimens from the southwestern Pacific suggest that this ultimate length is attained only after many years of steady growth, with the largest individuals often exceeding twenty kilograms in wet weight. Morphometric analyses indicate that the species displays a moderately deep body profile and a forked caudal fin, consistent with its pelagic, actively swimming lifestyle. Age determination based on otolith increment counts has proven reliable for this species, enabling researchers to construct robust growth curves linking length to age across the lifespan. The length-weight relationship, frequently described by the power-law equation W = aLᵇ where a is approximately 0.01413 in this population, provides a basis for converting field measurements of fork length into estimates of somatic mass. Such conversions are essential for fisheries stock assessments, as biomass estimates often rely on length-frequency data collected during commercial trawl surveys. The species is known to form loose aggregations over continental shelf habitats, where it preys upon small fishes and crustaceans, and it is considered a valuable target for both recreational and commercial fisheries throughout its temperate and subtropical range.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, female White trevally are characterised by a total length at puberty of 34.5 centimetres [Lp = 34.5 centimetres], a size typically reached between their second and third year of life. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for an individual of this length is approximately 504 grams [Wwp = approximately 504 grams], based on the established length-weight relationship for this species. This mass threshold signals the diversion of resources from somatic growth toward gonadal development, a shift that is accompanied by the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from individuals spanning this size range confirms the presence of developing oocytes, and the attainment of this size is considered a reliable proxy for the initiation of the reproductive life history stage. In the waters off eastern Australia and New Zealand, spawning aggregations of mature Pseudocaranx dentex form during the austral spring and summer months, when water temperatures are most favourable for egg and larval survival. The investment in reproduction at this size is substantial, though it represents only a fraction of the species' ultimate somatic capacity.

The spawning output of Pseudocaranx dentex is considerable; reproductively active females release a maximum of approximately 603 eggs per day during the peak of the spawning season at a water temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C], yielding an annual fecundity that can reach tens of thousands of eggs per individual [Ri = annual fecundity that can reach tens of thousands of eggs per individual]. Field studies using plankton nets to collect recently spawned eggs from the vicinity of known aggregation sites have validated this daily fecundity estimate, which is derived from counts of hydrated oocytes in gravid females. The spawning period extends for several months, meaning that a single female may release tens of thousands of pelagic eggs over the course of a single breeding season. Each egg measures approximately 1 millimetre in diameter and is buoyant, features that facilitate dispersal by ocean currents. From the egg diameter, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], reflecting the small initial size that typifies pelagic-spawning carangids. This minuscule mass imposes a high energetic cost on the parent, as the yolk reserves must provide sufficient nutrition for the embryo to develop through the cleavage and blastula stages until hatching.

Egg hatching, or eclosion, in Pseudocaranx dentex occurs after an incubation period of 7.5 days [ab = 7.5 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, is highly dependent on its endogenous yolk supply during the first few days following chorion rupture, as the mouth is not yet fully functional. The period of endotrophic nutrition is brief, and by approximately the third day post-hatching, the larva begins its exotrophic transition, actively seeking small planktonic prey. Larval survival during this critical phase is strongly influenced by water temperature, prey density, and the absence of predators. The relatively rapid development time to first exogenous feeding at this temperature is consistent with reports for other subtropical carangids and contrasts with the longer incubation periods observed in colder-water congeners. Following the onset of feeding, the pelagic larva grows rapidly, undergoing flexion and the development of fin rays before eventually settling into a demersal juvenile habitat. The total duration of the larval phase is a critical bottleneck in the species' population dynamics.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Pseudocaranx dentex is approximately 49 years [am = approximately 49 years], based on validated otolith readings from individuals collected in temperate waters at a mean annual water temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C]. This longevity is exceptionally high among carangid fishes and suggests a life history strategy that prioritises somatic persistence and repeated, iteroparous spawning events over a short, semelparous reproductive burst. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of the species, representing the maximum body mass recorded for adult individuals, is 21,172 grams [Wwi = 21,172 grams], a figure that underscores the substantial growth potential accumulated over decades. Such a large body size likely confers advantages in terms of fecundity, as fecundity scales positively with female mass in most teleosts, and may also reduce vulnerability to predation from smaller piscivores. The trade-off inherent in this strategy involves a delayed onset of reproduction, as the species does not begin spawning until it has accumulated considerable somatic tissue, but the pay-off is a prolonged reproductive window that can span several decades, contributing many cohorts to the population over an individual's lifetime.
